title: Lung cancer
seen_note: 436A — listed only ("lung cancer"); 441F — as previous gift
scenario: An elderly smoker with chronic cough who recently developed haemoptysis and weight loss; PA & lateral CXR + CT. Archive
A 60-year-old heavy smoker with dry cough and SOB for 4 months and two attacks of haemoptysis; CXR + CT (same pictures every year). 435 · 437A · 438F · Archive
Lung cancer discussion station (picture). Old exam

imgs.cap: CXR — irregular opacity, right lower zone (the repeated exam picture) Contrast CT chest (mediastinal window) — right lung mass
PA CXR — right lower-zone opacity (elderly smoker)

qs.q: Describe what you see in the images (CXR, CT).
a: CXR (PA): irregular opacification / radiopaque area in the lower zone of the right lung (say "zone" — you can't name the lobe without a lateral film).
CT chest with contrast (mediastinal window): homogeneously enhancing lesion in the right lung.
qs.why: Describe modality, side and zone (lobe needs a lateral view) and the lesion's features; CT gives size, enhancement and relations.

qs.q: What are the important points in the history? (cough/haemoptysis)
a: Haemoptysis: onset, duration, frequency, amount (spoonfuls), fresh/old, clots or streaks, with mucus, smell.
Associated: SOB, chest pain, fever/chills, joint pain (rheumatoid), voice change; anaemia & constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, appetite).
TB contact; bleeding elsewhere; previous lung disease, bleeding disorders; drugs
(anticoagulants); family history of lung cancer.
Smoking (pack-years), occupation (asbestos — e.g. plumber), travel.
qs.why: Characterise the haemoptysis, look for malignancy (weight loss, smoking pack-years), infection (TB contact, fever) and systemic disease.
hist: Chronicity and pattern of the bleeding.
Massive haemoptysis is life-threatening (airway) and needs urgent management.
Fresh or old, clots or streaks, with mucus, smell
Streaks in sputum suggest infection or tumour; foul smell suggests abscess or bronchiectasis.
Rheumatoid or vasculitis, or hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement by a lung tumour.
Weight loss and night sweats suggest cancer or TB.
TB is an important cause of haemoptysis.
A systemic cause of the bleeding.
The main risk factor for lung cancer.
Asbestos → mesothelioma and lung cancer; travel → TB and other infections.

qs.q: What is the most likely differential diagnosis?
a: Neoplastic: primary (SCLC / NSCLC) or metastasis.
Infectious: TB, abscess, fungal. Autoimmune: sarcoidosis, rheumatoid nodule.
qs.why: A lung mass in a smoker is cancer until proven otherwise; infection (TB, abscess) and inflammatory nodules are the alternatives.

qs.q: What are the types of lung cancer?
a: Small-cell; non-small-cell: squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, large-cell (bronchoalveolar).
qs.why: The split matters for treatment: small-cell is treated with chemotherapy; non-small-cell (squamous, adenocarcinoma, large-cell) is treated by stage, surgery when early.

qs.q: What is the next step to confirm the diagnosis? / Further investigations?
a: Sputum cytology, bronchoscopy (EBUS-guided FNA if central), CT-guided percutaneous core (tru-cut) biopsy if peripheral.
qs.why: Tissue is needed: bronchoscopy (EBUS) for central lesions, CT-guided core biopsy for peripheral ones.

qs.q: What investigations will you use to stage the cancer?
a: CT chest-abdomen-pelvis with contrast, PET scan, bone scan, brain MRI (if neurological symptoms).
qs.why: Staging looks for spread to nodes (PET/EBUS), adrenals/liver (CT), bone and brain — it decides resectability.

qs.q: What is the management of this patient?
a: Stage I: surgery (IB ± adjuvant chemo). Stage II: surgery + adjuvant chemo.
Stage IIIA: (neoadjuvant chemo +) surgery. Stage IIIB / IV: chemo(radio)therapy — palliative. Small-cell lung cancer is an indication for chemotherapy.
qs.why: Early NSCLC is cured by surgery (± adjuvant chemo); locally advanced disease gets multimodal therapy; advanced disease and SCLC are treated systemically.

qs.q: What are the surgical options?
a: Lobectomy with lymph-node dissection, pneumonectomy, segmentectomy, wedge resection.
qs.why: Lobectomy with nodal dissection is the standard; pneumonectomy for central tumours; sublobar resection for small tumours or poor reserve.

title: Pneumothorax — spontaneous & tension
seen_note: 442B — same as previous" (+ explain how the water-seal drain works)
scenario: A 35-year-old male smoker comes to the ER with chest pain and SOB, stable vitals; X-ray shown. He refuses treatment, goes home, and returns hypotensive, tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Archive
A patient comes to the ER collapsing — do a primary & secondary survey and say you need an X-ray; the doctor then gives it. Archive
Tension pneumothorax station — management. 435
Pneumothorax and its management. 438B
Unmanned station: sudden SOB with right-sided pain, became tachycardic and hypotensive, trachea shifted to the left — look at the X-ray (5 written questions). 441A

imgs.cap: 441A exam X-ray + scenario — right tension pneumothorax (trachea shifted left) CXR — left pneumothorax with visible pleural edge

qs.q: Describe the X-ray / what is the diagnosis? (include right vs left)
a: Absent lung markings peripheral to a visible visceral pleural edge, collapsed lung,
mediastinal/tracheal shift away from the affected side → (441A) right tension pneumothorax.
qs.why: A visible pleural edge with no lung markings beyond it = pneumothorax; mediastinal shift away from that side means tension.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis? (stable smoker)
a: Spontaneous pneumothorax.
qs.why: A young smoker with sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness and no trauma = primary spontaneous pneumothorax (ruptured apical bleb).

qs.q: How many types of pneumothorax are there?
a: Simple (spontaneous: primary/secondary), tension (JVD, hypotension, tracheal shift), open (traumatic, sucking wound).
qs.why: Pneumothoraces are classified as simple (spontaneous), tension (one-way valve, mediastinal shift, shock) and open (chest wall defect).

qs.q: He comes back hypotensive and tachycardic — what is the diagnosis?
a: Tension pneumothorax.
qs.why: Rising pressure in the pleural space shifts the mediastinum and kinks the great veins → obstructive shock: hypotension and tachycardia.

qs.q: Is an X-ray required to make the diagnosis? (yes/no)
a: No — tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; treat immediately.
qs.why: Tension pneumothorax kills in minutes — it is diagnosed clinically and decompressed without waiting for an X-ray.

qs.q: What is your management? (initial + definitive, with anatomical sites)
a: ABC + high-flow O₂.
Initial: needle decompression (thoracostomy) — 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line.
Definitive: chest tube (tube thoracostomy) — 5th intercostal space, between anterior & mid- axillary lines ("safe triangle") → underwater-seal drain.
Open pneumothorax: 3-sided occlusive dressing, then chest tube.
qs.why: A needle converts tension into a simple pneumothorax immediately; a chest tube in the safe triangle is the definitive treatment.

qs.q: Which intercostal space, and how do you count the ribs?
a: Start counting from the sternal angle (angle of Louis = 2nd rib/2nd costal cartilage).
qs.why: The sternal angle marks the 2nd costal cartilage — count down from there to find each space.

qs.q: What is the size of the needle and the chest tube?
a: Needle: at least 5–7 cm long, 14-gauge cannula.
Chest tube (adult): haemothorax 36–40 Fr; pneumothorax ~24 Fr (doctor: 26–32 also correct).
qs.why: The needle must be long enough to reach the pleura through the chest wall; chest tubes are large for blood (to avoid clotting), smaller for air.

qs.q: What is the expected complication of needle thoracostomy?
a: Failure (catheter too short/kinked/dislodged), bleeding (intercostal/internal mammary vessels), lung injury, infection, recurrence → needs chest tube.
qs.why: Short catheters fail or kink; the needle can hit vessels or lung; a chest tube is always needed afterwards.

notes.t: ATLS 10th edition prefers needle decompression at the 4th/5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line in adults (2nd ICS MCL in children).

extra.q: Management of spontaneous pneumothorax & indications for surgery
a: First attack: < 30 % → conservative; > 30 % → chest tube. Recurrence → chest tube even if < 30 %. Surgery (VATS bullectomy/pleurodesis): recurrent, bilateral, only one lung, high-risk jobs (pilots, divers), air leak > 7 days.

bonus.stem: A 25-year-old man is stabbed in the chest. He is alert but short of breath with a "sucking" wound over the right anterior chest wall. Most appropriate immediate management before definitive treatment?
opts: A. Cover with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on all four sides
B. Cover with a dressing taped on three sides
C. Insert a chest tube immediately at the 5th intercostal space
D. Give high-flow O₂ and await surgical evaluation
bonus.ans: Answer: B — the 3-sided dressing acts as a flutter valve (4 sides can create a tension pneumothorax); then chest tube away from the wound.

title: Achalasia
scenario: A 65-year-old complaining of difficulty in swallowing for the last four months (discussion station). 430F · 438A · 439A

imgs.cap: Barium swallow — dilated oesophagus with smooth "bird's-beak" narrowing

qs.q: What type of investigation is in the picture?
a: Barium swallow.
qs.why: Swallowed contrast outlining the oesophagus on fluoroscopy = barium swallow.

qs.q: Describe the findings.
a: Dilated proximal oesophagus with smooth tapering at the LES — "bird's beak" / "rat tail" sign.
qs.why: A dilated oesophagus tapering smoothly to a narrow LES gives the "bird's beak" — typical of achalasia (an irregular stricture would suggest cancer).

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Achalasia.
qs.why: Smooth tapering with proximal dilatation and dysphagia to both solids and liquids = achalasia.

qs.q: What is the best diagnostic modality, and what are the findings?
a: Oesophageal manometry — mention all: aperistalsis of the body, high (hypertensive) LES pressure, failure of LES relaxation on swallowing.
qs.why: Manometry is the gold standard: aperistalsis and failure of LES relaxation define achalasia.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Medical (CCB/nitrates) — only for patients unfit for surgery: low efficacy, side-effects (oedema, headache, hypotension).
Endoscopic Botox injection — wears off (~6 months).
Pneumatic dilatation — risk of perforation and reflux; may recur.
Surgery: Heller's myotomy (± fundoplication); POEM.
qs.why: All treatments lower LES pressure: drugs and Botox are temporary, dilatation risks perforation, and Heller myotomy (with partial fundoplication to prevent reflux) or POEM gives the most durable result.

title: Oesophageal cancer & dysphagia
scenario: A 65-year-old with difficulty swallowing for the last 4 months — "How will you approach the patient?" (discussion station). 430A
Barium swallow picture (radiological features). Archive
Dysphagia history station. Archive

imgs.cap: Barium swallow — irregular stricture with shouldering (similar picture)
Barium swallow — irregular filling defect of the distal oesophagus (white arrows) with shelf (red arrows) Barium swallow — malignant stricture (430A)

qs.q: Take a dysphagia history. / How will you approach the patient?
a: Site, duration, onset (sudden/gradual), painful (odynophagia) or painless, persistent vs intermittent, progressive (solids → liquids), difficulty initiating swallow, nasal
regurgitation/choking, food sticking, position-related.
Foreign-body ingestion, neck swelling (compression), Horner's, regurgitation/cough/recurrent chest infection (aspiration), weight loss/night sweats/fever, respiratory symptoms, anaemia, voice change.
Past GERD, drugs, previous surgery (strictures), family history of oesophageal cancer, smoking & alcohol.
qs.why: Dysphagia history localises (oropharyngeal vs oesophageal), separates mechanical (solids → liquids, progressive) from motility (both from the start), and looks for red flags (weight loss) and aspiration.
hist: The level the patient points to (not always accurate) helps localise the lesion.
Short, progressive history suggests malignancy; sudden onset suggests a foreign body.
Pain suggests oesophagitis, infection or ulceration.
Progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids = mechanical obstruction (cancer); both solids and liquids from the start = motility disorder (achalasia).
Difficulty initiating swallow, nasal regurgitation, choking
Help localise and characterise the obstruction.
Weight loss, night sweats, fever, anaemia
Smoking and alcohol are the main risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma.

qs.q: What will you look for on examination?
a: Respiratory examination (aspiration pneumonia as a complication), signs of anaemia, cachexia, cervical/supraclavicular nodes, hepatomegaly.
qs.why: Look for complications (aspiration, anaemia, cachexia) and spread (supraclavicular nodes, hepatomegaly).

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Basic labs (CBC, LFT…), CXR, barium swallow, oesophagoscopy (OGD + biopsy),
endoscopic/endobronchial US (staging).
qs.why: Barium shows the stricture; OGD with biopsy gives histology; EUS/CT/PET stage the tumour.

qs.q: Describe the finding on the X-ray / radiological features.
a: Barium swallow: irregular circumferential filling defect (irregular stricture with
"shouldering"/shelf) and pre-stenotic dilatation.
qs.why: An irregular stricture with shouldered margins and proximal dilatation is the typical malignant pattern.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Oesophageal cancer.
qs.why: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss and an irregular stricture in an older patient = oesophageal cancer.

qs.q: How do you confirm the diagnosis?
a: Flexible oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) with biopsy.
qs.why: Only biopsy gives histology (squamous vs adenocarcinoma) — OGD sees and samples the lesion.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: By stage: T1N0 → surgery (oesophagectomy / endoscopic mucosal resection for very early). Locally advanced → neoadjuvant chemoradiation (CROSS) → restage → surgery (open or minimally invasive oesophagectomy — explain the procedure).
Metastatic (M1) → palliative chemo; dysphagia → stent or radiotherapy.
Upper-third tumours → definitive chemoradiotherapy without surgery.
qs.why: Treatment follows the stage and site: very early disease by endoscopic resection or surgery, locally advanced by neoadjuvant chemoradiation then oesophagectomy, metastatic by palliation of dysphagia.

qs.q: What causes the dysphagia?
a: Luminal obstruction by the tumour and invasion (of the wall/surrounding structures).
qs.why: The tumour narrows the lumen and infiltrates the wall, so food can't pass.

title: Chest tube & underwater-seal drain
scenario: Under-water seal drain and chest tube station. Archive
Picture of the device in the 441A unmanned station. 441A
Pneumothorax station — explain how the water-seal drain works. 442B

imgs.cap: Underwater-seal chest drain (Atrium Ocean) — 441A exam picture

qs.q: What is the device you see?
a: Underwater-seal chest drainage system (chest drain).
qs.why: A multi-chamber collection unit attached to a chest tube is an underwater-seal drainage system.

qs.q: What is a chest tube, and how is it inserted?
a: A hollow flexible tube placed in the pleural space to drain air, blood, pus, chyle or other fluid. 5th ICS, anterior/mid-axillary line (safe triangle — away from pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi): local anaesthetic, O₂, monitor, 2 cm incision over the rib, blunt dissection over the upper border of the rib into the pleura (blood/air/pus comes out), finger sweep for adhesions, insert tube, connect to the underwater seal, suture & CXR.
qs.why: The tube is inserted in the safe triangle by blunt dissection over the upper border of the rib (avoiding the neurovascular bundle under the rib above), with a finger sweep before insertion.

qs.q: What are the components of the underwater-seal drain, and how does it work? / What is each chamber used for?
a: Collection chamber — collects fluid/blood (measure the output).
Water-seal chamber — tube end under ~2 cm water: one-way valve (air escapes, can't return). Bubbling = air leak; swinging (tidaling) with breathing = patent tube.
Suction-control chamber — limits the applied suction (usually −20 cmH₂O).
Keep the bottle below chest level and never clamp a bubbling drain.
qs.why: The water seal is a one-way valve: air bubbles out on expiration but can't be sucked back; swinging confirms patency and bubbling shows an air leak; the suction chamber limits negative pressure.

qs.q: What are the complications of a chest tube?
a: Insertional: pain, bleeding/haemothorax (intercostal vessels), puncture of lung/solid organ (liver, spleen), intra-abdominal placement, subcutaneous emphysema.
Positional: blockage/kinking/dislodgement, re-expansion pulmonary oedema, bronchopleural fistula.
Infective: wound infection, empyema.
qs.why: Insertion can injure vessels, lung or abdominal organs; the tube can block or dislodge; rapid re-expansion causes pulmonary oedema; infection can follow.

extra.q: When do you remove the chest tube?
a: Indication resolved on CXR, no air leak (no bubbling), drainage of blood/pus ≈ 0 (serous < 300–400 mL/day acceptable).

title: Anterior mediastinal mass (thymoma / germ-cell tumour)
scenario: Mediastinal pathology — PA and lateral chest X-ray. Archive

A 22-year-old man has an X-ray for another problem; an anterior mediastinal mass is found incidentally. 439F A 35-year-old man with shortness of breath, difficulty swallowing and drooping of the eyelids; X-ray shown (same image as the exam). (new case) 442A

imgs.cap: PA & lateral CXR — anterior mediastinal mass (arrows)
442A exam image — PA & lateral CXR, anterior mediastinal mass
"When you find a mediastinal mass always ask for…"
Contents of the anterior, middle and posterior mediastinum

qs.q: What are your findings on the X-ray?
a: PA: opacity/widening with increased density in the left upper zone, slight tracheal deviation to the right. Lateral: opacity occupying the anterior mediastinum.
qs.why: On the PA film a mass silhouettes the mediastinal contour; the lateral film places it in the anterior mediastinum (filling the retrosternal space) — location narrows the differential.

qs.q: What are the borders of the anterior mediastinum?
a: Sternum anteriorly; pericardium & great vessels posteriorly; superiorly the plane of the sternal angle (T4/5); inferiorly the diaphragm; laterally the mediastinal pleura.
qs.why: Knowing the compartment boundaries lets you place the mass and name its typical causes.

qs.q: Give the differential diagnosis.
a: 4 T's: thymoma, teratoma (germ-cell tumour), thyroid (retrosternal goitre), "terrible" T-cell lymphoma.
qs.why: Anterior mediastinal masses are the "4 T's": thymoma, teratoma/germ-cell tumour, thyroid (retrosternal goitre) and lymphoma.

qs.q: What is the next investigation / further imaging?
a: CT chest (CT chest-abdomen-pelvis); MRI; testicular US in males (442A answer: CT CAP, MRI, US of testis).
qs.why: CT defines the mass and its relations; in a young man a mediastinal germ-cell tumour may be metastatic from the testis, so the testes are examined/scanned.

qs.q: What blood investigations do you want?
a: Tumour markers: LDH, AFP, β-hCG; acetylcholine-receptor antibodies.
qs.why: AFP and β-hCG separate non-seminomatous germ-cell tumours (raised) from seminoma; LDH reflects tumour burden; AChR antibodies support thymoma with myasthenia.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: 439F: seminoma (normal AFP & β-hCG; CT homogeneous without calcification).
442A: thymoma with myasthenia gravis — you have to say myasthenia gravis.
qs.why: Normal markers with a homogeneous mass in a young man favour seminoma; ptosis, dysphagia and dyspnoea (fatigable weakness) with an anterior mass = thymoma with myasthenia gravis.

qs.q: How do you get a definitive diagnosis? / Do you need a biopsy?
a: Generally CT-guided (tru-cut) needle biopsy.
439F seminoma scenario: the examiner's answer was "No, biopsy not indicated".
qs.why: Tissue diagnosis usually guides treatment (CT-guided core biopsy); some examiners accept no biopsy when markers and imaging are typical, or when a thymoma looks resectable (biopsy can seed the capsule).

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Seminoma: chemotherapy — name the drugs: BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin). Thymoma + MG: pyridostigmine/neostigmine; plasmapheresis (or IVIG) in myasthenic crisis or no response; thymectomy.
qs.why: Seminoma is highly chemosensitive (BEP). Thymoma is resected (thymectomy), which also improves myasthenia; MG itself is treated with anticholinesterases and plasmapheresis/IVIG in crisis.

tips.t: The doctor said to say "opacity" or "widening", not "mass".

title: Haemothorax
scenario: Chest X-ray with a left-sided opacity. Archive

qs.q: What are the abnormalities on this X-ray?
a: Homogeneous opacity in the left lower zone obliterating the costophrenic angle (fluid).
qs.why: Fluid collects at the base on an erect film, giving a homogeneous opacity that obliterates the costophrenic angle.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Haemothorax.
qs.why: Fluid in the chest after trauma is blood until proven otherwise — haemothorax.

qs.q: What are the possible sources of bleeding?
a: Intercostal vessels, internal mammary vessels, lung parenchyma, bronchial arteries, major pulmonary vessels, heart and great vessels.
qs.why: Most haemothoraces come from chest-wall vessels (intercostal, internal mammary) or lung; the heart and great vessels cause massive bleeding.

qs.q: What is the initial management?
a: ABC: secure the airway, high-flow O₂, maintain circulation (2 large-bore lines, blood). Chest tube in the 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line + volume replacement.
qs.why: Resuscitate and drain: a large-bore tube in the safe triangle evacuates blood, re-expands the lung and measures the bleeding rate.

qs.q: When is thoracotomy indicated?
a: Initial drainage ≥ 1500 mL (the file says > 1250 mL, or > 1000 mL with hypotension), or > 200 mL/h for 2–4 consecutive hours, or persistent instability/transfusion need.
qs.why: Large initial drainage or continuing loss means a bleeding vessel that won't stop on its own — thoracotomy to control it.

title: Flail chest
scenario: Flail chest station. Archive

qs.q: What is flail chest?
a: A segment of chest wall moving paradoxically because of two or more fractures in each of three or more consecutive ribs.
qs.why: When a segment of ribs is broken in two places, it loses continuity and moves inwards on inspiration (paradoxical movement).

qs.q: What is your management?
a: ABC, O₂; stabilise the segment (gloved hand → folded dressing taped securely), careful movement.

Good analgesia — epidural (bupivacaine) is best, or PCA (morphine) → then oral analgesia. Intubation & positive-pressure ventilation only if respiratory failure (the doctor said it is NOT the first answer).
qs.why: The real problem is the underlying lung contusion and pain-limited breathing: oxygen and excellent analgesia (epidural) allow effective breathing; ventilation only for respiratory failure.

a: Chest already open for another reason, bilateral/severe flail affecting oxygenation, failure to wean from the ventilator, other intrathoracic injury.

title: Pneumonia → empyema
scenario: A patient with cough, greenish sputum, SOB and fever. The doctor showed 2 CXRs and one chest CT. Archive

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Pneumonia.
qs.why: Productive cough with fever and breathlessness = pneumonia.

qs.q: What investigation would you like to do?
a: Chest X-ray.
qs.why: A CXR confirms consolidation and shows complications such as effusion.

qs.q: Describe the X-ray.
a: Blunting of the costophrenic angle with a meniscus sign → pleural effusion; (after chest tube, no improvement) → empyema.
qs.why: A meniscus with blunted costophrenic angle is a pleural effusion; persistence after drainage suggests a loculated empyema.

qs.q: What other investigation would you like to do?
a: CT chest; thoracocentesis (pleural tap) for fluid analysis.
qs.why: CT shows loculation and pleural thickening; pleural tap gives the fluid's character (pus, pH, glucose, culture).

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis now?
a: Empyema secondary to pneumonia.
qs.why: Pus in the pleural space after pneumonia = empyema.

qs.q: What is the treatment?
a: IV antibiotics (know the duration — some doctors asked) + chest-tube drainage; if it fails → surgical decortication (VATS/open) to allow lung re-expansion.
Repeat the CXR after the tube; no improvement → CT.
qs.why: Infected pleural fluid must be drained (chest tube) with prolonged antibiotics; if the lung is trapped by a fibrous peel, decortication frees it.

qs.q: How do you differentiate an exudate from a transudate?
a: Light's criteria — exudate if any: fluid/serum protein > 0.5; fluid/serum LDH > 0.6; fluid LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH.
qs.why: Light's criteria identify exudates (inflammation, infection, malignancy — high protein/LDH) versus transudates (heart, liver, kidney failure).
